content: Family medicine in the United States is distinct from the European concept of general practice. Physicians specializing in family medicine, often referred to as family physicians, must complete a three-year residency in family medicine after earning their medical degree. This additional training qualifies them for board certification, which is now a requirement for most hospitals and health plans. Family physicians typically work in solo or small-group private practices or as employees in hospital-owned practices of similar size. Some choose to teach medicine at medical schools or family medicine residency programs, often for lower compensation. Others may work as consultants for medical institutions, including insurance companies. Since the 1970s, many family physicians in the U.S. have viewed the terms general practitioner or GP as dismissive, as these terms fail to acknowledge their extended training. Family physicians are board-certified in family medicine, with training focused on providing care across all life stages. They are skilled in managing a wide range of medical issues, particularly common conditions, and many also deliver babies in addition to caring for patients of all ages. To become a family physician, one must complete undergraduate education, medical school, and three years of specialized residency training in family medicine. Board-certified family physicians must pass a written examination every six to ten years, depending on their chosen certification maintenance track. Additionally, they are required to complete 300 hours of continuing medical education within the prior six years to remain eligible for recertification. Between 2003 and 2009, the certification process transitioned to include annual tests covering various specialty areas. The American Board of Family Medicine now mandates ongoing participation in continuous learning and self-assessment to enhance clinical knowledge and skills. This is part of the Maintenance of Certification Program for Family Physicians (MC-FP), which evaluates proficiency in professionalism, lifelong learning, cognitive expertise, and practice performance. Family physicians can pursue Certificates of Added Qualifications (CAQs) in areas such as adolescent medicine, geriatrics, sports medicine, sleep medicine, and hospice and palliative care, provided they meet additional training and testing requirements. Fellowships are also available in fields like adolescent medicine, geriatrics, sports medicine, rural medicine, faculty development, hospitalist medicine, obstetrics, research, and preventive medicine. The family medicine paradigm is supported by primary care physicians trained in internal medicine, although these physicians primarily treat adult patients. In the U.S., there is a growing number of physicians dual-trained in internal medicine and pediatrics, a combined program that takes four years to complete instead of three years each for internal medicine and pediatrics. However, many family medicine practices, especially in suburban and urban areas, no longer provide obstetric services due to litigation concerns and provider preferences. This has blurred the distinction between family medicine and internal medicine/pediatrics. Internal medicine/pediatrics-trained physicians often lean toward subspecialty training or hospital-based practice, but there are collaborative practices where family medicine and internal medicine/pediatrics-trained physicians work seamlessly together. Physicians face increasing administrative burdens, higher malpractice premiums due to insurance monopolies, and a payment model that prioritizes patient volume over quality of care. These pressures reduce the time physicians can spend on patient care. As insurance carriers consolidate, the focus has shifted further toward volume, increasing insurance company profits. In response, some physicians are moving away from insurance-based models to reduce paperwork and focus on patient care, aligning with their original training. The average starting salary for family physicians in the U.S. ranges from $120,000 to $150,000 annually. A growing trend among family physicians is the adoption of a micro practice or Ideal Medical Practice model. These practices aim to reduce overhead costs and increase the use of technology, allowing physicians to see fewer patients while maintaining financial stability. This model enables doctors to spend more time with each patient, leading to higher satisfaction for both patients and physicians.
